name: Tunisian Brik
originStatus: Tunisia; canonical fried malsouka pastry. This version is brik à l’oeuf with tuna, capers, parsley, and potato.

ingredients.text: 1 medium floury potato, about 8 oz/225 g, peeled and cubed
1 tbsp finely chopped onion or scallion
1 can tuna in olive oil, about 5 oz/140 g, drained and flaked
4 malsouka or brik pastry sheets; 8-inch spring-roll wrappers are the best substitute

method: Boil the potato in salted water until tender, 10-12 minutes. Drain well, mash roughly, and cool. Mix with parsley, onion, capers, tuna, and the remaining salt.
Heat 1/2 inch/1.25 cm oil in a wide skillet to 350°F/175°C. Place one pastry sheet on a plate. Spoon one-quarter of the filling onto one half, making a shallow well in the center.
Crack an egg into the well, dot with harissa if using, fold the pastry into a half-moon or triangle, and immediately slide it into the oil. Hold the edge closed with tongs for several seconds.
Fry 60-90 seconds per side for a runny yolk, or slightly longer for a set yolk, until blistered and golden. Drain upright on paper towels. Repeat and serve at once with lemon.
accuracyNote: Filo can work only if doubled and lightly oiled; it is more fragile than malsouka. The egg should be added immediately before frying.

name: Egyptian Koshari
originStatus: Egypt; canonical layered street meal of rice, lentils, pasta, chickpeas, tomato sauce, garlic-vinegar daqqa, and fried onions.

ingredients.text: 3 large yellow onions, very thinly sliced
1 cup/200 g brown or green lentils, rinsed
8 oz/225 g small elbow macaroni or ditalini

method: Toss onions with flour and salt. Fry in batches at 340-350°F/170-175°C until deep golden. Drain; they crisp as they cool.

Simmer lentils in water until barely tender, 15-20 minutes; drain. Brown vermicelli in 2 tbsp oil, add rice, lentils, cumin, salt, and 2 1/4 cups/530 ml water. Cover and cook on low 15 minutes; rest 10 minutes.
Boil pasta until al dente. For the sauce, fry garlic and spices briefly, add paste and tomatoes, simmer 20 minutes, then add vinegar and salt.
Simmer daqqa ingredients 3 minutes. Layer rice-lentils, pasta, chickpeas, tomato sauce, and onions. Serve daqqa and extra chile sauce alongside.
accuracyNote: The separate tangy daqqa is central to Cairo-style koshari and should not be omitted.

name: Maakouda Potato Fritters
originStatus: Morocco and Algeria; canonical potato fritter or sandwich filling.

ingredients.text: 1 1/4 lb/570 g floury potatoes, peeled and cubed
2 tbsp fine breadcrumbs, only if mixture is loose
Harissa, lemon, and bread, for serving

method: Boil potatoes in salted water until tender. Drain thoroughly and return to the hot pan for 1 minute to evaporate moisture. Mash and cool until just warm.
Mix in garlic, herbs, cumin, turmeric, pepper, salt, and egg. If too soft to shape, add breadcrumbs a tablespoon at a time. Chill 20 minutes.
Shape into 2-inch/5 cm patties about 1/2 inch/1.25 cm thick. Dust lightly with flour and shake off excess.
Heat 1/2 inch/1.25 cm oil to 350°F/175°C. Fry in batches 2-3 minutes per side until crisp and golden. Drain and salt lightly.
Serve with lemon and harissa, or tuck into khobz with tomato, onion, olives, and sauce.
accuracyNote: Some Moroccan versions dip the patties in a thin yeast-flour batter; the simpler flour-coated form is equally established. Thoroughly drying the potatoes prevents breakage.

name: Merguez in Khobz
originStatus: Maghrebi-French street sandwich; grilled merguez in North African bread.

ingredients.text: 12 small merguez sausages, about 1 1/4 lb/570 g total
4 small rounds khobz, batbout, or crusty demi-baguettes
1 cup slata mechouia or roasted pepper-tomato salad
1/3 cup harissa diluted with 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp lemon juice
1/2 cup green olives, pitted and chopped, optional

method: Heat a charcoal grill, grill pan, or skillet over medium-high. Prick neither the sausages nor their casings; losing fat makes them dry.
Grill merguez, turning frequently, until browned and the center reaches 160°F/71°C, usually 8-10 minutes. Rest 3 minutes.
Warm and split the bread without cutting all the way through. Spread with diluted harissa.
Fill each with slata mechouia, onion, herbs, olives, and three sausages. Spoon over a little sausage juice and serve immediately.
accuracyNote: Merguez is traditionally lamb or lamb-beef sausage seasoned with chile, garlic, cumin, coriander, and sometimes caraway. A baguette reflects the French-Maghrebi version; khobz gives a more North African presentation.

name: Bocadillo de Calamares
originStatus: Madrid, Spain; not North African. Included with corrected attribution.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g cleaned squid tubes and tentacles
1/4 cup/35 g rice flour, optional for extra crispness
Neutral or mild olive oil, for frying
4 crusty Spanish-style rolls or small baguettes
Garlic mayonnaise, optional and nontraditional in the simplest Madrid version

method: Slice squid tubes into 1/2-inch/1.25 cm rings. Pat every surface very dry; moisture causes splattering and a gummy coating.
Heat 2 inches/5 cm oil to 365°F/185°C. Mix flours and salt. Toss squid lightly in the mixture and shake off all excess.
Fry in small batches for 60-90 seconds, only until pale gold and just tender. Overcooking makes squid rubbery. Drain and season immediately.
Split the bread and fill generously with hot squid. Serve plain in the classic style, with lemon at the table; add garlic mayonnaise only if desired.
accuracyNote: Madrid’s classic is intentionally spare: crisp fried squid and bread. Thick batter and heavily sauced versions are later variations.

name: Sfenj Doughnuts
originStatus: Morocco and neighboring Maghreb; canonical unsweetened yeast doughnut.

ingredients.text: 1 2/3 cups/395 ml lukewarm water, plus up to 3 tbsp as needed
Neutral oil, for frying and handling
Granulated sugar or warm honey, optional

method: Mix flour, yeast, salt, sugar, and water into a very sticky, elastic dough. Beat vigorously by hand or with a paddle 8-10 minutes; it should stretch in strands and remain wetter than bread dough.
Cover and rise until doubled and bubbly, 60-90 minutes. Wet or oil hands and gently fold the dough several times.

Heat 2 inches/5 cm oil to 350°F/175°C. Keep a bowl of water or oil nearby. Pinch off a small orange-sized piece, poke a hole through the center, stretch into a rough ring, and lower carefully into oil.
Fry 2-3 at a time, turning repeatedly, until deep golden and cooked through, about 4 minutes. Drain.
Serve hot and plain, dusted with sugar, or dipped briefly in honey.
accuracyNote: Traditional sfenj is minimally sweet or unsweetened; its character comes from the wet dough, chewy open crumb, and crisp exterior.

name: Bessara Fava Soup
originStatus: Northern Morocco; canonical dried split-fava puree served as soup or dip.

ingredients.text: 2 cups/400 g dried split, peeled fava beans, rinsed
6 cups/1.4 L water, plus more as needed
1 tsp cumin, plus more for serving
1/3 cup/80 ml extra-virgin olive oil, divided

method: Combine favas, water, garlic, and salt. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer partly covered until the beans collapse, 45-60 minutes. Stir often near the end to prevent scorching.
Blend until completely smooth, adding hot water to achieve a pourable soup or leaving it thick for a dip.
Return to low heat. Stir in cumin, paprika, cayenne, and half the olive oil. Simmer 5 minutes and adjust salt.
Ladle into bowls. Make a small well in each and pour in remaining olive oil. Dust with cumin and paprika; serve with lemon and bread.
accuracyNote: Split peas are used in some households and regional versions, but dried split fava beans define classic Moroccan bessara.

name: Hawawshi
originStatus: Egypt; canonical meat-stuffed baladi bread. This is the common Cairo-style method using pita-like bread rather than the Alexandrian dough-enclosed version.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g ground beef or lamb, 15-20% fat
1 small onion, very finely chopped and squeezed dry
6 small aish baladi or pita breads
3 tbsp olive oil or melted ghee

method: Heat oven to 450°F/230°C with a sheet pan inside. Mix meat, onion, pepper, chile, parsley, garlic, and spices until evenly combined, without compacting excessively.
Split each bread enough to open the pocket. Spread a thin, even layer of meat, about 1/4 inch/6 mm thick, all the way to the edges.
Brush both sides with oil. Place on the hot pan and cover with a second pan or parchment and another tray to keep flat.
Bake 8 minutes, flip, then bake 6-8 minutes more until crisp and the filling reaches 160°F/71°C. Rest 3 minutes before cutting.
accuracyNote: A thin filling cooks safely before the bread burns. Alexandrian hawawshi encloses the filling in raw dough and requires a different bake.

name: Ta’ameya Falafel
originStatus: Egypt; canonical fava-bean falafel, notably greener and lighter than chickpea falafel.

ingredients.text: 2 cups/360 g dried split peeled fava beans, soaked 12-18 hours and drained
1/2 cup dill fronds, optional but common
1 tsp baking powder, added just before frying

method: Process drained favas, scallions, herbs, garlic, coriander, cumin, and salt in batches to a fine, damp meal. Do not puree into paste. Chill 30 minutes.
Heat oil to 350°F/175°C. Stir baking powder into only the portion being fried.
Shape heaped tablespoons into flattened rounds. Press one face into sesame seeds.
Fry in batches, sesame-side down first, 3-4 minutes total until dark golden and cooked through. Drain.
Serve in aish baladi with tahini, tomato, cucumber, pickles, and chile sauce.
accuracyNote: Authentic Egyptian ta’ameya is principally made from dried fava beans, not canned beans. Raw soaked beans provide the correct texture and bind.

name: Fricassé Sandwich
originStatus: Tunisia; canonical fried yeast bun filled with tuna, potato, egg, olives, capers, and harissa.

ingredients.text: Harissa thinned with olive oil and lemon

method: Knead dough ingredients until smooth and elastic, 8 minutes. Cover and rise until doubled, about 1 hour.
Divide into 10 pieces and shape as short oval rolls. Proof 20-30 minutes.
Fry at 340°F/170°C, turning, until evenly deep golden and cooked through, 4-5 minutes. Drain and cool until easy to handle.
Split without cutting through. Spread generously with harissa, then fill with potato, egg, tuna, olives, capers, and optional slata mechouia.
accuracyNote: Fricassé is a fried bun, not a baguette sandwich and not the French stewing method of the same name.

name: Chapati Zanzibari
originStatus: Zanzibar and the Swahili coast of East Africa; not North African. A layered, pan-cooked flatbread shaped by Indian Ocean trade.

ingredients.text: 3 tbsp coconut oil, ghee, or neutral oil
Additional oil for layering and cooking

method: Mix flour, salt, sugar, oil, and enough water to make a soft dough. Knead 8-10 minutes until smooth. Cover and rest 30 minutes.

Divide into eight balls. Roll one ball thinly into a large circle, brush with oil, then roll tightly into a rope. Coil the rope into a snail shape and tuck the end underneath. Repeat and rest 15 minutes.
Roll each coil into a 7-inch/18 cm round, preserving the layers.
Cook on a medium-hot dry skillet until bubbles form. Brush lightly with oil, flip, and cook both sides until mottled brown and flaky, 2-3 minutes total.
Stack under a towel to keep pliable.
accuracyNote: The coil-and-roll technique creates the characteristic Swahili layered texture. Coconut oil is especially fitting for Zanzibar.

name: Karantita
originStatus: Oran, Algeria; canonical baked chickpea-flour custard, usually served hot in bread with cumin and harissa.
yieldText: One 9 x 13-inch/23 x 33 cm pan, 8 servings

ingredients.text: 1/3 cup/80 ml neutral or olive oil
1 tsp ground cumin, plus more for serving

method: Whisk chickpea flour and water until smooth. Rest 30-60 minutes so the flour hydrates.
Heat oven to 425°F/220°C. Whisk oil, eggs, salt, pepper, and cumin into the batter. It will be thin.
Oil a metal baking pan and pour in batter to a depth of about 1 inch/2.5 cm.
Bake 35-45 minutes until the center is softly set and the top is well browned, blistered, and slightly puffed. Broil briefly if needed.
Cool 10 minutes. Spoon or slice into baguette, dust heavily with cumin, and add harissa.
accuracyNote: Texture should be tender and custardy, not dry like cornbread. Eggless versions are also traditional.

name: Mahjouba Semolina Crêpe
originStatus: Algeria; canonical mhadjeb/mahjouba, a thin semolina flatbread folded around tomato-onion filling.

ingredients.text: 3 ripe tomatoes, grated or finely chopped

method: Cook onions in olive oil over medium-low until very soft, 15 minutes. Add garlic, tomatoes, paste, spices, harissa, and salt. Cook until thick and almost dry; cool completely.
Knead semolina, salt, and enough water into a very soft, elastic dough, 10-12 minutes. Divide into eight oiled balls and rest 30 minutes.
On an oiled surface, stretch one ball paper-thin into a large square. Place a thin layer of filling in the center and fold all four sides over to make a flat parcel.
Cook on a lightly oiled griddle over medium heat, 3-4 minutes per side, until browned, flaky, and cooked through.
accuracyNote: A dry, cooled filling is essential; watery tomato tears the delicate dough.

name: Grilled Sardine Skewers
originStatus: Coastal Maghreb; traditional ingredients and technique, though the skewer presentation varies by port and household.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g fresh sardines, scaled, gutted, heads removed, butterflied if desired

method: Soak wooden skewers 30 minutes. Pat sardines dry. Mix oil, garlic, spices, salt, herbs, and half the lemon juice.
Coat fish lightly and marinate in the refrigerator 15-20 minutes only; longer acid exposure softens them.
Thread sardines crosswise onto paired skewers so they do not spin. Heat grill very hot and oil the grate.
Grill 2-3 minutes per side until the skin crisps and flesh turns opaque. Finish with remaining lemon juice.
accuracyNote: Freshness is decisive: sardines should smell clean, have bright eyes, and firm flesh. Paired skewers make fragile fish easier to turn.

name: Snail Babbouche Broth
originStatus: Morocco, especially Marrakech street stalls; canonical snail broth with a complex herb-and-spice infusion.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g food-grade live or pre-cleaned edible snails
1 tbsp coarse salt, plus more for cleaning
1 small piece dried licorice root, optional

method: Buy snails intended for cooking. Follow the supplier’s purging instructions. Wash repeatedly in cold water and coarse salt until no slime remains; rinse thoroughly.
Put snails in a pot with cold water and slowly bring to a simmer so they emerge from shells. Skim carefully.
Add salt, whole spices, licorice, bay, orange peel, tea, thyme, mint, and chile. Simmer partly covered 1 1/2 hours, until snails are tender and broth aromatic.
Taste and adjust salt. Serve snails and broth in small bowls with toothpicks.
accuracyNote: Do not use garden snails exposed to pesticides or unidentified species. Keep raw snails separate from ready-to-eat foods and boil thoroughly.

name: Msemen with Amlou
originStatus: Morocco; canonical flaky griddled flatbread served with the Souss almond-honey-argan spread.

ingredients.text: 1/3 cup melted butter mixed with 1/3 cup oil

method: Knead flour, semolina, salt, yeast, and water into a smooth, supple dough, 10 minutes. Divide into eight oiled balls; rest 20 minutes.
Grind almonds until they release oil and become a smooth butter. Blend in argan oil, honey, and salt. Set aside.
On an oiled surface, stretch each dough ball nearly transparent. Brush with butter-oil, dust lightly with semolina, fold opposite sides toward center, then fold again into a square. Rest 10 minutes.
Flatten gently and griddle over medium heat, turning several times, until crisp, layered, and cooked through, 5-7 minutes.
Serve warm, torn and dipped into amlou.
accuracyNote: Use culinary, not cosmetic, argan oil. Msemen dough relies on extensive kneading and resting rather than a large amount of yeast.

name: Feseekh Rolls
originStatus: Contemporary serving format based on Egyptian feseekh, the traditional salt-cured fermented mullet eaten particularly at Sham el-Nessim. The roll format is not a canonical historic dish.

ingredients.text: 8 oz/225 g commercially produced feseekh from a reputable refrigerated supplier
4 small aish baladi or thin flatbreads
1 small red onion, very thinly sliced

method: Keep feseekh refrigerated. Open in a well-ventilated area. Remove skin, bones, head, and dark viscera; use only firm flesh.
Flake the flesh and toss with abundant lemon juice. Let stand refrigerated 10 minutes. Lemon improves flavor but does not make unsafe fish safe.
Warm bread briefly. Layer greens, tomato, onion, parsley, small amounts of feseekh, and optional chile. Drizzle with olive oil and roll tightly.
Serve immediately; discard leftovers that have sat out more than 2 hours.
accuracyNote: Do not make feseekh at home from these instructions. Improperly fermented salted fish has caused botulism. Pregnant people, older adults, young children, and immunocompromised people should avoid it.

name: Lablabi Chickpea Bowl
originStatus: Tunisia; canonical chickpeas and broth ladled over torn stale bread with harissa, cumin, lemon, olive oil, and optional egg or tuna.

ingredients.text: 2 cups/400 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight
Tuna, capers, olives, and chopped parsley, optional

method: Drain chickpeas. Simmer with water and half the garlic until very tender, 75-90 minutes. Add salt late in cooking. Reserve abundant broth.
Pound remaining garlic with cumin and a pinch of salt. Stir into the hot chickpea broth and simmer 5 minutes.
Put torn bread in deep bowls. Ladle over chickpeas and enough broth to soften without turning soupy.
Let diners season with harissa, lemon, olive oil, and extra cumin. Add egg, tuna, capers, olives, or parsley as desired.
accuracyNote: Lablabi is assembled to taste at the table. Day-old bread is intentional and absorbs the garlicky cumin broth.

name: Kebda Iskandarani
originStatus: Alexandria, Egypt; canonical spicy liver sandwich filling with garlic, cumin, chile, and vinegar.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g beef or calf liver, trimmed and sliced into thin strips
4 aish fino rolls or small baguettes
Tahini, tomato, pickles, and parsley, optional

method: Pat liver very dry. Heat a heavy skillet over high until smoking lightly. Add oil and liver in one uncrowded layer.
Sear 60-90 seconds before stirring. Add garlic, chile, cumin, coriander, pepper, and salt. Cook 2-3 minutes more, until browned outside but not chalky.
Add vinegar and lemon; toss 30 seconds while scraping the pan. Remove promptly.
Fill warm rolls and add pickles, tomato, parsley, or a thin smear of tahini.
accuracyNote: Thin slicing and very high heat prevent toughness. Liver should be cooked through according to local food-safety guidance but not held on heat after doneness.

name: Zaalouk Baguette
originStatus: Contemporary sandwich presentation of canonical Moroccan zaalouk, a cooked eggplant-tomato salad. Baguette service reflects Moroccan-French urban eating.
method: Char whole eggplants under a broiler or over gas until collapsed and smoky, turning often. Cool, peel, and drain 10 minutes; chop.
Cook olive oil, garlic, tomato, paprika, cumin, cayenne, and salt in a skillet until reduced and jammy, 12-15 minutes.
Add eggplant and herbs. Mash with a spoon and cook until thick enough to hold on bread, 10 minutes. Finish with lemon and cool to warm.
Split and toast baguette. Fill with zaalouk; add olives or a thin streak of harissa if desired.
accuracyNote: Zaalouk should be concentrated, not watery. Charred eggplant gives a smokier regional variation; boiling or roasting is also traditional.

name: Batbout Sliders
originStatus: Modern mini-sandwich format using canonical Moroccan batbout skillet bread.

ingredients.text: Filling choice: kefta, maakouda, grilled vegetables, tuna, or chicken

method: Knead flour, semolina, yeast, sugar, salt, and water into a soft smooth dough, 8-10 minutes. Cover and rise 45 minutes.
Roll 1/4 inch/6 mm thick. Cut 3-inch/7.5 cm rounds. Place on semolina-dusted cloth, cover, and proof 20-30 minutes.
Heat a heavy griddle over medium. Cook rounds without oil, turning every 30-45 seconds, until puffed and spotted, 4-5 minutes.
Cool under a towel. Split pockets and fill just before serving so breads do not become soggy.
accuracyNote: Frequent turning encourages an even pocket. Batbout is pan-cooked rather than baked like standard khobz.

name: Chakchouka Wrap
originStatus: Modern wrap built from Maghrebi chakchouka/shakshuka. Tunisia and Algeria have numerous pepper-tomato-egg versions.

ingredients.text: 4 large msemen, lavash, or flour flatbreads

method: Cook onion and peppers in oil over medium until soft and lightly browned, 10-12 minutes. Add garlic, tomatoes, paprika, cumin, harissa, and salt.
Cook until very thick and nearly dry, 12-15 minutes. Make four wells, add eggs, cover, and cook until whites set and yolks are soft.
For a rollable filling, break the eggs into the sauce and cook another minute so no loose white remains. Cool 3 minutes.
Spoon onto warm flatbreads, add herbs, fold sides inward, and roll. Toast seam-side down in a dry skillet.
accuracyNote: Reducing the sauce more than for a plated chakchouka prevents a soggy wrap. The wrap itself is a contemporary presentation.

name: Fried Whitebait Cornet
originStatus: Mediterranean coastal street-food presentation; common in North African port cities but not one standardized national recipe.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g cleaned whitebait or very small smelt

method: Rinse fish quickly and dry extremely well. Mix flour, semolina, salt, cumin, and paprika.
Heat oil to 365°F/185°C. Toss fish lightly in coating and shake in a sieve to remove excess.
Fry in small batches 2-3 minutes until crisp and pale golden. Drain, salt, and keep uncovered.
Serve immediately in parchment cones with lemon and optional sauce on the side.
accuracyNote: Small fish are often eaten whole after gutting if necessary. Do not pile or cover after frying; trapped steam destroys crispness.

name: Harira Night Cup
originStatus: Modern small-cup presentation of canonical Moroccan harira, traditionally prominent at sunset during Ramadan.

ingredients.text: 8 oz/225 g lamb or beef, finely diced, optional
3 tbsp flour whisked with 1 cup/240 ml water

method: Brown meat lightly in oil if using. Add onion, celery, herbs, and spices; cook 5 minutes.
Add tomatoes, chickpeas, lentils, and stock. Simmer until lentils and meat are tender, 40-50 minutes.
Add vermicelli. Slowly stir in flour slurry and simmer 10-12 minutes, stirring, until silky and lightly thickened.
Season with salt and lemon. Serve in heatproof cups with dates and bread alongside.
accuracyNote: The cup is only a serving format. Harira’s recognizable structure is tomato, pulses, herbs, warming spices, noodles or rice, and a flour-based thickener called tedouira.

name: Mombar Rice Sausage
originStatus: Egypt; canonical stuffed beef or sheep intestine filled with seasoned rice and herbs, then simmered and fried.

ingredients.text: 6 ft/1.8 m cleaned food-grade beef or sheep casing
Coarse salt, flour, and vinegar for cleaning
1 1/2 cups/300 g short-grain rice, rinsed and drained
1 cup chopped parsley, cilantro, and dill
Stock, bay leaf, and onion for simmering

method: Turn casings inside out and scrub repeatedly with coarse salt and flour; rinse, soak briefly in diluted vinegar, and rinse again. Follow supplier instructions.
Mix rice, onion, tomatoes, herbs, paste, spices, salt, and oil. Fill casings only halfway using a funnel; rice expands. Tie into 5-inch/12 cm links and prick each once with a fine needle.
Lower into gently simmering seasoned stock. Cook 45-60 minutes until rice is tender and casing cooked. Drain and cool.
Shallow-fry until crisp and browned, 6-8 minutes. Serve hot with lemon.
accuracyNote: Keep casings cold and sanitary. Overfilling can burst links; vigorous boiling can also split them.

name: Kaak Warka Rings
originStatus: Tunisia, especially Zaghouan; canonical delicate ring pastry filled with almond and perfumed with rose or orange-blossom water.

ingredients.text: 1/2 cup/115 g clarified butter or melted unsalted butter
2 cups/220 g finely ground blanched almonds
2 tbsp rose water or orange-blossom water

method: Rub butter into flour and salt. Add just enough warm water to form a smooth dough. Knead briefly, cover, and rest 30 minutes.
Mix filling into a firm paste. Roll into pencil-thick ropes about 4 inches/10 cm long.
Roll dough paper-thin. Cut strips slightly wider than filling. Wrap each almond rope, seal with a dab of water, trim excess, and join ends into a ring.
Bake at 325°F/165°C for 15-20 minutes. The pastries should remain pale with only faint coloring underneath.
Cool completely before storing airtight.
accuracyNote: Kaak warka is prized for a thin white shell and smooth almond center; browning it deeply changes the intended texture and appearance.

name: Grilled Corn with Cumin
originStatus: North African street-style seasoning; grilled corn itself is widespread rather than belonging to one canonical national formula.

ingredients.text: 2 tbsp olive oil or melted butter

method: Heat a charcoal or gas grill to medium-high. Rub corn lightly with oil.
Grill, turning every 2 minutes, until kernels are tender and charred in spots, 10-12 minutes.
Mix cumin, salt, paprika, and cayenne. Sprinkle over hot corn and squeeze with lemon.
Add cilantro if desired and serve immediately.
accuracyNote: Cumin and salt are common Maghrebi street seasonings. The recipe is intentionally simple and should taste of smoke, corn, cumin, and citrus.

name: Douara Offal Skewers
originStatus: Modern skewer interpretation of Maghrebi douara, which more commonly means a stew of tripe and other offal. Clearly labeled as an adaptation.
method: Simmer cleaned tripe in salted water until tender, 1 1/2-2 hours. Drain, cool, and cut into 1-inch/2.5 cm pieces.
Trim heart and cut heart and liver into similar pieces. Combine oil, garlic, spices, salt, and lemon. Marinate all offal refrigerated 30 minutes.
Thread pieces by type or alternate them, noting liver cooks fastest. Grill over high heat, turning often. Remove liver when just cooked, 4-6 minutes; heart and precooked tripe may take 8-10 minutes.
Ensure all pieces are safely cooked, sprinkle with parsley, and serve with bread and harissa.
accuracyNote: Source offal from a regulated butcher, prevent cross-contamination, and use a thermometer where practical. This is not the standard stewed douara preparation.

name: Sardine Chermoula Roll
originStatus: Modern sandwich format based on Moroccan sardines with chermoula, a classic pairing.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g sardine fillets, pin bones removed

method: Coat sardines with half the chermoula and refrigerate 15 minutes. Pat lightly so they remain seasoned but not dripping.
Dust with flour or semolina. Shallow-fry at 350°F/175°C, 1-2 minutes per side, until crisp and just cooked. Drain.
Spread bread with remaining chermoula. Layer tomato, onion, greens, and sardines.
Finish with lemon and serve immediately.
accuracyNote: Sardines and chermoula are traditional; the bread-roll construction is a practical contemporary street-food treatment.

name: Roasted Chestnut Cone
originStatus: Mediterranean and North African winter street snack; presentation is traditional to many regions but not exclusive to the Maghreb.
method: Heat oven to 425°F/220°C. With a chestnut knife or sturdy paring knife, cut a deep X through the shell on the rounded side of every chestnut. This prevents bursting and permits peeling.
Toss with water and optional salt. Spread in one layer on a heavy tray.
Roast 20-30 minutes, shaking twice, until shells curl back and nuts are tender.
Wrap briefly in a clean towel to steam. Serve hot in paper cones and peel while still warm.
accuracyNote: Discard chestnuts that smell sour, show mold, or remain hard and shriveled after roasting. Street vendors may roast over charcoal or in perforated drums for smokier flavor.

name: Chicken M’qualli with Preserved Lemon
originStatus: Morocco; a canonical m’qualli-style chicken tagine seasoned with ginger, saffron, preserved lemon, and olives.

ingredients.text: 1 whole chicken, 3 1/2-4 lb/1.6-1.8 kg, cut into 8 pieces
1 1/2 tsp salt, less if the preserved lemon and olives are salty
Large pinch saffron threads, crumbled into 2 tbsp warm water
2 large onions, finely chopped or grated
1 cup/240 ml water or unsalted chicken stock
1 preserved lemon, pulp discarded, rind rinsed and cut into strips
1 cup/150 g green or purple Moroccan olives, rinsed

method: Season the chicken with salt, ginger, turmeric, pepper, and saffron water. Heat the oil in a heavy pot or tagine base and brown the pieces lightly, 6-8 minutes total; remove.
Add onions, garlic, cilantro, and parsley. Cook over medium-low heat until the onions soften, 10 minutes. Return the chicken and add the water.
Cover and simmer gently, turning once, until the breast reaches 165°F/74°C and the legs are tender, 35-50 minutes. Remove the chicken and keep warm.
Add preserved-lemon rind and olives. Boil the onion sauce uncovered until thick and glossy, 10-15 minutes. Return the chicken, coat with sauce, and adjust acidity with lemon juice.
accuracyNote: A traditional m’qualli sauce should be onion-rich, concentrated, and yellow-gold rather than watery. Some cooks briefly broil or roast the chicken before serving for browned skin.

name: Lamb M’hammar
originStatus: Morocco; festive lamb that is first braised with aromatics and then browned, giving the dish its name from the Arabic root associated with reddening or browning.

ingredients.text: 4 lb/1.8 kg bone-in lamb shoulder or shanks
Large pinch saffron, soaked in 2 tbsp warm water
1 tsp ground cinnamon, optional in sweeter regional versions

method: Rub lamb with salt, ginger, pepper, turmeric, and saffron water. Melt butter with oil in a Dutch oven and color the lamb lightly on all sides.
Add onions, garlic, herbs, and water. Cover and braise at 325°F/165°C, turning occasionally, until very tender, 2-2 1/2 hours.
Transfer lamb to a roasting tray. Reduce the onion cooking liquid until jammy; stir in cinnamon and honey only when making the sweet-leaning version.
Roast or broil the lamb at 450°F/230°C until deeply browned and crisp at the edges, 10-15 minutes. Spoon the reduced onion sauce around it.
accuracyNote: M’hammar is a technique family, not one fixed seasoning formula. The defining sequence is moist cooking followed by pronounced browning.

name: Kefta Mkaouara
originStatus: Morocco; small kefta meatballs simmered in spiced tomato sauce, often finished with eggs.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g ground beef, lamb, or a mixture
1/3 cup finely chopped parsley and cilantro
1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry
1 1/2 lb/680 g ripe tomatoes, grated, or one 28-oz/800-g can crushed tomatoes

method: Mix kefta ingredients gently and roll into 3/4-inch/2-cm balls. Refrigerate while making the sauce.
Heat oil in a wide tagine or skillet. Soften onion and garlic, then add tomatoes, spices, salt, and herbs. Simmer uncovered until thickened, 20 minutes.
Nestle meatballs into the sauce, cover, and cook gently 10-12 minutes, shaking the pan rather than stirring. Confirm the centers reach 160°F/71°C.
Make four wells, crack in eggs, cover, and cook until whites set but yolks remain soft, 4-7 minutes. Serve with bread.
accuracyNote: Breadcrumbs are unnecessary in the compact, small Moroccan kefta used here. Eggs are common but optional.

name: Seven-Vegetable Couscous
originStatus: Morocco; Friday couscous whose exact seven vegetables vary by season and household.

ingredients.text: 3 cups/500 g medium couscous, not instant if steaming traditionally
1 1/2 lb/680 g lamb shoulder or beef chuck, optional
1/2 small green cabbage, cut into wedges
1 lb/450 g pumpkin or winter squash, in large pieces

method: In the bottom of a couscoussier, brown meat lightly in oil. Add onions, tomatoes, chickpeas, spices, herb bundle, and water. Simmer 45 minutes.
Moisten couscous with 1 cup/240 ml cool salted water, rubbing grains apart with oiled hands. Rest 10 minutes, then steam uncovered over the broth until vapor rises through it, about 20 minutes.
Turn couscous into a wide bowl, sprinkle with another 3/4 cup/180 ml water, separate the grains, cool briefly, and steam again. Add carrots, turnips, cabbage, and sweet potato to the broth.
Repeat moistening and steam a third time while adding zucchini and pumpkin for the final 20-25 minutes. Work smen into the couscous.
Mound couscous, arrange meat and vegetables, and moisten with broth. Serve extra broth separately.
accuracyNote: “Seven” is culturally meaningful but not a rigid botanical count; onion, tomato, chickpeas, and herbs may or may not be included in a household’s tally.

name: Lamb Tangia
originStatus: Marrakesh, Morocco; a slow-cooked bachelor or tradesmen’s dish traditionally sealed in an urn-shaped clay vessel and cooked in the embers of a hammam furnace.

ingredients.text: 3 1/2 lb/1.6 kg boneless lamb shoulder, in large chunks
1 preserved lemon, pulp removed and rind sliced

method: Heat oven to 300°F/150°C. Combine all ingredients in a tangia jar, bean pot, or tightly covered Dutch oven. The meat should fit snugly.
Cover with parchment and foil before applying the lid to minimize evaporation. Bake 4-4 1/2 hours, turning the meat once if using a Dutch oven.
Uncover when the lamb is spoon-tender. If liquid is abundant, transfer it to a saucepan and reduce to a rich emulsion; return it to the meat.
Serve directly from the vessel with bread.
accuracyNote: Classic tangia is austere: lamb, preserved lemon, cumin, saffron, garlic, smen, and olive oil. Added vegetables or dried fruit turn it into a different tagine style.

name: Beef Tagine with Prunes
originStatus: Morocco; celebratory sweet-savory tagine, commonly made with beef or lamb and garnished with sesame or fried almonds.

ingredients.text: 2 1/2 lb/1.1 kg beef chuck, cut into 2-inch/5-cm pieces
1/3 cup toasted sesame seeds or fried blanched almonds

method: Season beef with salt, ginger, turmeric, pepper, and saffron. Brown in oil in batches. Add onions, garlic, cinnamon sticks, and water.
Cover and simmer very gently until tender, 1 3/4-2 hours, adding small amounts of water as needed.
In a separate pan, cover prunes with some of the beef broth. Add honey and ground cinnamon; simmer until plump and syrupy, 10-15 minutes. Add orange blossom water off heat.
Reduce the beef sauce until it coats the meat. Arrange prunes over the beef and garnish with sesame or almonds.
accuracyNote: Cooking the fruit separately keeps it intact and lets the meat sauce remain savory before the elements are combined.

name: Fish Tagine Chermoula
originStatus: Morocco; fish marinated in chermoula and baked or gently simmered over vegetables.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g firm fish fillets or steaks, such as cod, sea bass, snapper, or monkfish
1 lb/450 g potatoes, sliced 1/4 inch/6 mm thick and parboiled 5 minutes

method: Coat fish with half the chermoula and refrigerate 30 minutes. Heat oven to 375°F/190°C.
Oil a tagine or baking dish. Layer onion, potatoes, tomatoes, and peppers, seasoning lightly and spooning over half the remaining chermoula.
Set fish on top. Add preserved lemon, olives, water, oil, and the final chermoula.
Cover and bake 25 minutes, then uncover until fish flakes and reaches about 145°F/63°C, 10-15 minutes more. Avoid overcooking.
accuracyNote: Potato thickness and par-cooking matter because fish cooks much faster than raw potatoes.

name: Chicken Pastilla
originStatus: Fez and broader Morocco; an elaborate sweet-savory pie traditionally made with warqa pastry, poultry, onion-egg custard, and cinnamon almonds.

ingredients.text: 3 lb/1.35 kg bone-in chicken thighs and breasts
2 cups/280 g blanched almonds, fried or toasted
Confectioners’ sugar and cinnamon, for garnish

method: Braise chicken with butter, onions, spices, herbs, and water until tender and 165°F/74°C, about 45 minutes. Remove meat, discard bones and skin, and shred.
Reduce the onion liquid until thick. Slowly stir in beaten eggs over low heat until softly curdled and nearly dry. Cool separately from the chicken.
Pulse almonds with sugar, cinnamon, and orange blossom water to coarse crumbs.
Heat oven to 375°F/190°C. Butter a 10-inch pan. Overlap buttered pastry sheets so edges hang over. Layer chicken, egg-onion mixture, and almonds. Fold over pastry and cap with additional sheets.
Bake until crisp and deep gold, 35-45 minutes. Rest 10 minutes, invert if desired, and dust decoratively with confectioners’ sugar and cinnamon.
accuracyNote: Keep the three fillings relatively dry and cool before assembly; excess moisture destroys the pastry’s crispness.

name: Rfissa with Fenugreek
originStatus: Morocco; postpartum and celebratory dish of chicken, lentils, fenugreek, and fragrant broth served over shredded trid or msemen.

ingredients.text: 2 tbsp fenugreek seeds, soaked overnight and drained
1 whole chicken, 3 1/2-4 lb/1.6-1.8 kg, cut up
1 tsp ras el hanout or m’sakhen blend
10-12 plain msemen or trid sheets, cooked and torn into strips

method: Put chicken, onions, oil, smen, spices, salt, herbs, and water in a large pot. Simmer covered 30 minutes.
Add lentils and drained fenugreek. Continue gently until chicken is cooked and legumes are tender, 35-50 minutes. Remove chicken and reduce broth slightly; it should remain plentiful.
Steam torn msemen or trid briefly over the broth, or warm in a covered pan with a few spoonfuls of broth.
Mound bread strips on a platter, moisten thoroughly with broth, and top with lentils, onions, fenugreek, and chicken. Serve extra broth alongside.
accuracyNote: Fenugreek should perfume rather than dominate. Soaking reduces bitterness, and trid is the canonical base; torn msemen is a common practical substitute.

name: Djej Bil Zaytoun
originStatus: Algeria and Tunisia; “chicken with olives,” made in several white, saffron, or tomato-tinged regional styles. This is a light Algerian-style version.

ingredients.text: 2 carrots, cut into thick coins, optional
1 tbsp flour mixed with 2 tbsp water, optional

method: Season chicken with salt, ginger, pepper, and turmeric. Brown lightly in olive oil; remove.
Soften onion and garlic. Add carrots, stock, and chicken. Cover and simmer until tender and 165°F/74°C, 35-45 minutes.
Blanch olives in fresh water for 5 minutes if very salty. Add to the pot for the final 15 minutes.
Thicken lightly with flour slurry only if needed. Finish with parsley and lemon juice.
accuracyNote: Olive salinity varies dramatically. Rinsing or blanching prevents an over-salted sauce.

name: Mrouzia Honey Lamb
originStatus: Morocco; Eid al-Adha preserve-style tagine of lamb, ras el hanout, honey, raisins, and almonds.

ingredients.text: 4 lb/1.8 kg lamb neck, shoulder, or shanks
1 cup/140 g fried or toasted almonds

method: Coat lamb with salt and spices. Brown lightly in butter, then add onions, cinnamon sticks, and water.
Cover and simmer until nearly tender, 1 3/4-2 1/2 hours depending on the cut.
Add raisins, honey, and ground cinnamon. Cook uncovered over low heat, turning the lamb carefully, until the sauce becomes thick, dark, and lacquered, 25-40 minutes.
Garnish with almonds and sesame.
accuracyNote: Mrouzia should balance spice and sweetness and historically kept well because its sauce was intensely reduced; modern versions still require refrigeration.

name: Chtitha Djej
originStatus: Algeria; chicken in a red dersa sauce of garlic, paprika or chile, cumin, and chickpeas.
method: Pound garlic with paprika, hot pepper, cumin, black pepper, salt, and 1 tbsp water to form a dersa paste.
Brown chicken in oil. Add dersa and tomato paste and fry 1 minute without scorching.
Add water, cover, and simmer 30 minutes. Add chickpeas and cook until chicken reaches 165°F/74°C and sauce is reduced, about 15 minutes more.
Finish with lemon and herbs.
accuracyNote: Dersa is the dish’s defining flavor base; onions are absent or minimal in many Algerian versions.

name: Loubia White Bean Stew
originStatus: Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia; white beans in a tomato, garlic, cumin, and paprika sauce, vegetarian or enriched with meat.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g dried cannellini or navy beans, soaked overnight
1 1/2 tsp salt, plus more to taste

method: Drain beans. Soften onion in oil, add garlic, tomato paste, tomatoes, and spices, and cook 5 minutes.
Add beans and water. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer partially covered until creamy-tender, 60-90 minutes. Add water if necessary.
Salt fully once beans begin to soften. Stir in herbs for the final 10 minutes.
Adjust with lemon and olive oil. Serve with bread.
accuracyNote: Dried beans give the best broth. Canned beans can be substituted and simmered in the sauce for about 25 minutes.

name: Molokhia with Rabbit
originStatus: Egypt; chopped jute-mallow leaf soup served with rabbit. This is distinct from Tunisia’s long-cooked, powdered-leaf mloukhia stew.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g frozen chopped molokhia leaves, thawed, or 1 1/2 lb/680 g fresh leaves, finely chopped

method: Simmer rabbit with onion, bay, cardamom, salt, and water until tender and at least 160°F/71°C in the thickest portion, 60-90 minutes. Strain and reserve 5 cups/1.2 L broth. Brown rabbit in ghee if desired.
Bring broth to a gentle simmer. Stir in molokhia and heat without a hard boil, 5-8 minutes; vigorous boiling can dull its green color and texture.
For ta’leya, fry garlic and coriander in ghee until fragrant and just golden. Pour into the soup and stir once.
Serve with rabbit, rice or bread, and lemon.
accuracyNote: Egyptian molokhia is deliberately mucilaginous and soup-like. Powdered Tunisian mloukhia requires a completely different, hours-long method.

name: Fasolia Green Bean Stew
originStatus: Egypt and the eastern Arab Mediterranean; green beans braised in tomato, with or without beef or lamb.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g beef chuck or lamb shoulder, cubed, optional
1 1/2 lb/680 g green beans, trimmed and cut

method: If using meat, brown it in ghee. Add onion and cook until soft; add garlic, tomato paste, and spices.
Add tomatoes and stock. Cover and simmer until meat is nearly tender, about 60 minutes.
Add green beans and cook partially covered until tender but intact, 25-35 minutes. For a vegetarian stew, begin with the onions and simmer beans in the tomato sauce for 35-45 minutes.
Adjust salt and finish with cilantro.
accuracyNote: The sauce should cling to the beans rather than resemble tomato soup. Frozen green beans need less cooking.

name: Camel Meat Tagine
originStatus: Saharan Morocco and neighboring desert regions; camel meat is consumed regionally, but there is no single universal camel tagine formula. This version uses Moroccan savory tagine technique.

ingredients.text: 3 lb/1.35 kg food-inspected camel shoulder or stew meat, trimmed and cubed

method: Season camel with salt and spices. Brown in oil in batches.
Add onions, garlic, herbs, preserved lemon, and water. Cover and braise at a bare simmer or at 325°F/165°C until very tender, generally 2 1/2-3 1/2 hours.
Add olives for the final 20 minutes. Remove the meat and reduce the sauce until concentrated.
Return meat to glaze and serve with bread or couscous.
accuracyNote: Camel age and cut strongly affect tenderness. Use only legally inspected meat and cook tough shoulder cuts as a stew until collagen has fully softened.

name: Quince & Lamb Tagine
originStatus: Morocco; autumn sweet-savory tagine pairing lamb with aromatic quince.
method: Braise lamb with salt, spices, butter, onions, cinnamon sticks, and water until tender, 1 1/2-2 hours.
Scrub and quarter quinces, remove cores, and hold pieces in acidulated water. Poach in some lamb broth until just tender, 15-25 minutes.
Transfer quince to a skillet with honey, cinnamon, lemon, and 1/2 cup broth. Cook until glazed and rose-gold.
Reduce lamb sauce until thick. Arrange quince over lamb and spoon over its syrup.
accuracyNote: Quince remains firm until cooked and oxidizes rapidly once cut. Poaching it separately prevents it from disintegrating in the meat braise.

name: Artichoke & Pea Tagine
originStatus: Morocco; spring tagine of artichoke bottoms and peas, often with lamb or beef but equally coherent as a vegetable dish.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g lamb or beef cubes, optional

method: If using meat, brown it in oil. Add onion, garlic, spices, herbs, and water and simmer until nearly tender, 60-75 minutes. For vegetarian preparation, simmer the aromatics with 2 cups vegetable stock for 20 minutes.
Add artichoke bottoms and cook until tender, 15-25 minutes depending on type.
Add peas, preserved lemon, and lemon juice; cook 8-10 minutes more.
Reduce sauce gently and adjust salt.
accuracyNote: Frozen artichoke bottoms are a more accurate substitute than canned marinated hearts, which are acidic and texturally different.

name: Bakoula Mallow Stew
originStatus: Morocco. Despite the supplied title, bakoula is normally served as a cooked mallow or mixed-greens salad, not a liquid stew. The corrected preparation follows that tradition.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g cleaned common mallow leaves, or a mix of spinach and chard

method: Positively identify and wash mallow repeatedly. Steam or cook it with only the clinging water until tender, 15-20 minutes. Drain and chop.
Put greens, herbs, garlic, paprika, cumin, cayenne, salt, and oil in a skillet.
Cook over medium-low heat, stirring and mashing, until moisture evaporates and the mixture becomes cohesive, 15-20 minutes.
Stir in preserved lemon, olives, and lemon juice. Serve warm or at room temperature.
accuracyNote: Never forage mallow unless identification and growing conditions are certain. Spinach-chard is the safest accessible substitute, though less mucilaginous.

name: Chicken with Almonds & Eggs
originStatus: Moroccan celebratory-style chicken with reduced onion sauce, fried almonds, and hard-cooked eggs; household names and spice profiles vary.

ingredients.text: 1 whole chicken, 4 lb/1.8 kg, cut into pieces
3 tbsp butter and olive oil combined

method: Season chicken. Brown lightly in butter-oil; add onions, garlic, herbs, and water.
Cover and simmer until chicken reaches 165°F/74°C, 35-50 minutes. Remove chicken and reduce onions to a thick sauce.
Fry almonds at 325°F/165°C until pale gold; drain immediately. Brown chicken briefly under the broiler if desired.
Arrange chicken with onion sauce, eggs, and almonds. Dust very lightly with cinnamon only if customary in the intended household style.
accuracyNote: This is a descriptive family of festive Moroccan presentations rather than a uniquely standardized national dish.

name: Sardine Meatball Tagine
originStatus: Morocco, especially coastal cities; sardine kefta simmered in tomato chermoula sauce.

ingredients.text: 1/3 cup/60 g cooked rice or 1/4 cup breadcrumbs, optional binder

method: Pulse sardines, herbs, garlic, spices, and optional rice just until minced. Chill 15 minutes, then form walnut-size balls with wet hands.
Simmer oil, garlic, tomatoes, paste, spices, and water until slightly thick, 15 minutes.
Gently add sardine balls in one layer. Cover and simmer without vigorous stirring for 10-12 minutes, until opaque and firm.
Add preserved lemon and olives for the final 5 minutes.
accuracyNote: Do not purée the fish to paste; a lightly minced texture produces tender sardine kefta.

name: Kaddid Dried Beef Couscous
originStatus: Tunisia, Libya, and Algeria; couscous enriched with kaddid or gueddid, salt-dried meat. This home recipe begins with commercially produced, inspected dried meat.

ingredients.text: 12 oz/340 g commercially cured kaddid or gueddid

method: Soak kaddid in several changes of cold water for 4-8 hours, then simmer 20 minutes and discard that water if still excessively salty.
Fry onion, tomato paste, harissa, and spices in oil. Add meat, chickpeas, and water and simmer 45 minutes.
Add firm vegetables. Steam couscous over the broth in two or three stages as directed in Recipe 34, adding zucchini and pumpkin late.
Taste before adding salt. Serve meat and vegetables over couscous with broth.
accuracyNote: Home meat drying carries microbial and curing risks. Use a regulated product unless following a professionally validated curing process.

name: Marqa Hlowa Sweet Stew
originStatus: Tunisia and Algeria; literally a “sweet sauce/stew,” typically meat with prunes, raisins, apricots, and nuts. Formulas differ by city and holiday.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g lamb or beef, in large cubes
1/4 cup/85 g honey or sugar, to taste

method: Brown meat in butter. Add onion, cinnamon, turmeric, pepper, salt, and water. Cover and simmer until tender, 75-100 minutes.
Add prunes, apricots, raisins, and honey. Simmer uncovered until fruit is plump and sauce syrupy, 15-25 minutes.
Remove from heat and add orange blossom water.
Garnish with almonds.
accuracyNote: This should be sweet but still taste of meat and spice; add honey gradually because dried-fruit sweetness varies.

name: Osban Stuffed Tripe
originStatus: Tunisia and Libya; cleaned tripe casings filled with rice, herbs, chickpeas, spices, and chopped offal or meat, then simmered.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g professionally cleaned sheep tripe, cut into 6-inch/15-cm pouches
1/2 lb/225 g lamb liver, finely diced
1/2 lb/225 g lamb shoulder or heart, finely diced
1 cup/165 g cooked chickpeas, roughly chopped
1 cup chopped parsley, cilantro, and dill
8 cups/1.9 L seasoned tomato broth or couscous broth

method: Rinse cleaned tripe in cold water and inspect carefully. Mix liver, meat, raw rice, chickpeas, onion, herbs, paste, harissa, spices, and oil.
Sew or tie three sides of each pouch. Fill only halfway; rice expands significantly. Close securely and prick each pouch once or twice with a sterile skewer.
Lower into barely simmering broth. Cook gently 1 1/2-2 hours, turning carefully, until casing is tender and filling reaches at least 165°F/74°C.
Rest 10 minutes before slicing. The broth may be used for couscous.
accuracyNote: Buy tripe already cleaned under sanitary commercial conditions. Underfilling prevents bursting; hard boiling can split the casing.

name: Chakhchoukha Ravioli Stew
originStatus: Algeria. The supplied “ravioli” description is inaccurate: chakhchoukha uses torn, thin rougag or trid flatbread under a spicy lamb-and-chickpea stew.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g lamb shoulder or shanks
10-12 sheets rougag or very thin unleavened flatbread, torn

method: Brown lamb in oil. Add onions, garlic, tomato paste, spices, and salt; cook 5 minutes. Add water and simmer 60 minutes.
Add chickpeas and firm vegetables. Add zucchini and pumpkin only for the final 20 minutes. Cook until lamb is tender and broth flavorful.
Steam torn rougag briefly over the stew or warm it in a covered dish.
Spread bread on a platter and ladle over enough red broth to soften it without flooding. Top with meat, chickpeas, and vegetables.
accuracyNote: Rougag absorbs sauce rapidly, so assemble immediately before eating.

name: Dfina Sabbath Stew
originStatus: Moroccan Jewish; slow-cooked Sabbath stew related to skhina and dafina, with beef, chickpeas, potatoes, grains, and shell-on eggs.

ingredients.text: 2 cups/330 g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight
2 lb/900 g beef brisket or chuck
1 whole garlic head, top sliced off
1 cup/190 g wheat berries or barley, tied loosely in cheesecloth
1-2 tbsp honey or date syrup, optional
Water to cover by 1 inch/2.5 cm

method: Heat oven to 225°F/107°C. Put drained chickpeas in a heavy covered pot, then arrange beef, potatoes, onion, garlic, grain parcel, and eggs.
Add spices, salt, oil, optional sweetener, and enough water to cover. Bring to a full simmer on the stovetop for 10 minutes.
Cover tightly and transfer to the oven for 12-16 hours. Check before sleep or after the first 3 hours and add boiling water if ingredients are exposed.
By serving time, meat should be tender, eggs brown, and broth mostly absorbed. Peel eggs and serve components separately or together.
accuracyNote: Religious households arrange cooking according to Sabbath observance and local rabbinic practice. For food safety, the pot must remain continuously above 140°F/60°C after reaching a simmer.

name: Berkoukes Pearl Couscous
originStatus: Algeria and Morocco; hand-rolled large semolina pellets cooked in a hearty vegetable, chickpea, and often meat broth.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g lamb or beef cubes, optional
2 cups/340 g berkoukes or moghrabieh-size semolina pearls

method: Brown meat in oil if using. Add onion, celery, garlic, tomato paste, and spices and cook 5 minutes.
Add water, chickpeas, carrots, and turnip. Simmer until meat is nearly tender, about 60 minutes.
Add zucchini and berkoukes. Simmer, stirring frequently, until pearls are tender, 15-25 minutes; add hot water if the stew becomes too thick.
Stir in cilantro and adjust seasoning.
accuracyNote: True berkoukes is larger and more irregular than Israeli couscous, but the latter can substitute with a shorter cooking time.

name: Lamb & Cardoon Tagine
originStatus: Morocco and Algeria; spring-winter tagine using the fleshy ribs of cultivated cardoon.
method: Brown lamb in oil. Add onion, garlic, spices, herbs, and water; simmer covered 75 minutes.
Strip strings from cardoon ribs, cut into 3-inch/7.5-cm pieces, and hold in water acidulated with half the lemon. Boil separately in salted lemon water until partly tender, 20-30 minutes; drain.
Add cardoon to lamb and cook until both are tender, 25-35 minutes.
Add preserved lemon, olives, and remaining lemon juice; reduce sauce.
accuracyNote: Use cultivated culinary cardoon, not an unidentified wild thistle. Cardoon requires stringing and pre-cooking to tame bitterness and toughness.

name: Squid & Chickpea Marqa
originStatus: Tunisia; tomato-harissa marqa with squid and chickpeas, representative of coastal home cooking.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g cleaned squid, bodies cut into rings and tentacles separated

method: Cook onion in oil until soft. Add garlic, tomato paste, harissa, tabil, paprika, and caraway and fry 2 minutes.
Add water, chickpeas, and potatoes and simmer 15 minutes.
Add squid. Either cook very briefly, 3-4 minutes, for a lighter stew, or simmer gently 35-45 minutes until tender; avoid the rubbery middle interval.
Adjust salt and finish with parsley and lemon.
accuracyNote: Long-simmered squid is common in marqa; it becomes tender again after its initial tightening phase.

name: Goat Tagine with Figs
originStatus: A plausible Moroccan and Maghrebi regional combination rather than one nationally standardized recipe; slow-braised goat is paired here with dried figs and warm spices.

ingredients.text: 3 lb/1.35 kg bone-in goat shoulder or stew pieces
12 oz/340 g dried figs, stems removed

method: Season goat with salt and spices. Brown in oil; add onions, garlic, and water.
Cover and braise at 325°F/165°C or a bare simmer until almost tender, 1 3/4-2 1/2 hours.
Soak figs in hot water 15 minutes. Add to the pot with honey and cook uncovered until goat is fully tender and sauce is glossy, 20-30 minutes.
Balance with lemon juice and garnish with almonds.
accuracyNote: Goat may require longer than lamb. The dish is best treated as a carefully labeled regional-style adaptation, not presented as a singular canonical Moroccan tagine.

name: Shakshuka
originStatus: North African, especially Tunisian and Libyan, with later widespread Israeli adoption; eggs poached in a reduced tomato-pepper sauce.

ingredients.text: 1 can whole peeled tomatoes, 28 oz/800 g, crushed by hand

method: Cook onion and peppers in olive oil over medium heat until very soft and lightly browned, 12-15 minutes.
Add garlic, cumin, paprika, caraway, and harissa; stir 1 minute. Add tomatoes and salt and simmer uncovered until thick enough to hold wells, 15-20 minutes.
Make six wells and crack in the eggs. Cover and cook on low until whites set but yolks remain soft, 5-8 minutes.
Scatter with herbs and serve immediately with bread.
accuracyNote: The sauce must be reduced before the eggs are added; a watery base produces steamed rather than properly poached eggs.

name: Mafroum Stuffed Potatoes
originStatus: Libyan and Tunisian Jewish; paired potato slices are stuffed with meat, battered, fried, and then braised in tomato sauce. Also called m’battan batata in Libya.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g ground beef or lamb
1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry

method: Slice potatoes lengthwise into 1/3-inch/8-mm slabs. Cut a pocket into each slab or pair two smaller slices. Soak in salted water 20 minutes, then dry.
Mix meat, grated onion, parsley, garlic, paprika, cinnamon, pepper, and 1/2 tsp salt. Fill potato pockets without overstuffing.
Dip in beaten egg, then flour. Shallow-fry at 350°F/175°C until golden on both sides; the meat need not yet be cooked through.

In a wide pot, soften sliced onion in olive oil. Add paste, tomatoes, water, turmeric, and remaining salt. Arrange mafroum snugly in one layer, cover, and simmer 45-60 minutes, until potatoes are tender and meat reaches 160°F/71°C.
accuracyNote: Frying sets the stuffed potato before braising; skipping that step makes the pieces prone to falling apart.

name: Pkaila Spinach & Beans
originStatus: Tunisian Jewish; a dark, intensely cooked spinach or chard concentrate forms the base of a beef-and-bean stew, also called tfina pkaila.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g spinach or Swiss chard leaves, washed and very well dried
1 cup/240 ml neutral or olive oil
1 lb/450 g dried white beans, soaked overnight
1 cup/170 g small pasta or semolina dumplings, optional

method: Chop greens very finely. Cook with oil over low heat, stirring often, until moisture evaporates and the mixture turns nearly black-green and paste-like, 1 1/2-2 1/2 hours. Do not burn. Drain off and reserve excess oil.
Brown beef lightly in 2 tbsp reserved oil. Add onion, garlic, herbs, spices, salt, beans, 1 cup pkaila concentrate, and water.
Cover and simmer very gently until beef and beans are tender, 2-2 1/2 hours. Add water as needed.
Add small pasta only for the final 15-20 minutes. The finished stew should be dark, rich, and thick.
accuracyNote: Pkaila’s characteristic color comes from prolonged controlled cooking, not scorching. Commercial pkaila concentrate is commonly used and greatly shortens preparation.

name: Chraime Spiced Fish
originStatus: Libyan Jewish; firm fish steaks cooked in a fiery red garlic, paprika, cumin, and tomato sauce, commonly served for Sabbath and holidays.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g firm fish steaks or thick fillets, such as cod, halibut, grouper, or carp

method: Season fish with salt and lemon. Heat olive oil gently; cook garlic until fragrant but not brown.
Add paprika, hot pepper, cumin, and tomato paste. Stir 30 seconds, then immediately add water and optional sugar. Simmer 10 minutes.
Nestle fish into sauce in one layer. Cover and simmer gently until just opaque and about 145°F/63°C, 8-15 minutes depending on thickness.
Add cilantro and let stand 10 minutes before serving.
accuracyNote: Paprika burns easily and becomes bitter; add liquid promptly after blooming the spices.

name: Skhina Sabbath Stew
originStatus: Moroccan Jewish; skhina, s’hina, or dafina refers to the same broad family of overnight Sabbath stews. This version emphasizes separate rice and wheat parcels.

ingredients.text: 2 1/2 lb/1.1 kg beef brisket, chuck, or short ribs
1 tbsp honey or date syrup, optional

method: Place rice and wheat separately in loosely tied heat-safe cloth bags with enough room to expand; season each lightly.
Arrange chickpeas, beef, potatoes, sweet potato, onion, garlic, eggs, and grain bags in a heavy pot. Add spices, oil, optional sweetener, and boiling water to cover.
Bring to a simmer for 10 minutes, cover tightly, and bake at 225°F/107°C for 12-16 hours.
Ensure liquid remains sufficient during the first few hours. Serve meat, vegetables, eggs, chickpeas, rice, and wheat as distinct components.
accuracyNote: Skhina and dafina are overlapping names, not separate fixed recipes. Keeping grains in cloth bundles preserves their identity during overnight cooking.

name: Mina de Matza
originStatus: Sephardic Passover pie made from softened matzo layered around meat, spinach, leek, eggplant, or cheese filling. This meat version is dairy-free.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g ground beef or lamb
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water, for top

method: Heat oven to 350°F/175°C. Soften matzo briefly in warm stock, one sheet at a time; it should bend without dissolving.
Cook onion in oil until soft. Add meat and brown thoroughly. Add garlic, spices, salt, pepper, and parsley; cook until nearly dry, then cool slightly and stir in three beaten eggs.
Oil a 9-inch springform or baking dish. Layer half the matzo, overlapping to line the bottom and sides. Add filling and cover with remaining matzo.
Brush with egg wash and bake until firm and browned, 40-50 minutes. Rest 15 minutes before cutting.
accuracyNote: Mina is a Sephardic Passover form with many regional fillings; it should not be claimed as exclusively North African.

name: Boyos de Pan
originStatus: Rhodian/Ottoman-Sephardic cheese biscuits made with soaked stale bread, flour, egg, oil, butter, and hard cheese. This is not a Moroccan dish.

ingredients.text: 10 slices white sandwich bread, preferably stale, crusts optional
1 tbsp olive or neutral oil, plus more for brushing
1 cup/100 g finely grated Parmesan or aged kasseri
2 cups/250 g all-purpose flour, plus more as needed

method: Heat oven to 400°F/200°C. Soak bread in water, then squeeze it extremely dry.
Mix bread, butter, oil, cheese, flour, egg, and salt into a uniform, soft dough. Add a little flour only if too sticky to shape.
Form 30 golf-ball-size pieces, place on a lined tray, and flatten with fork tines.
Brush lightly with oil, sprinkle with cheese, and bake until golden, about 20 minutes.
accuracyNote: The title is used differently across Ottoman-Sephardic communities. This version follows the documented Rhodes “cheese biscuit” preparation, not İzmir’s laminated boyoz pastry.

name: Sfenj for Hanukkah
originStatus: Moroccan and North African Jewish Hanukkah tradition; the doughnut itself is the same airy, unsweetened sfenj eaten more broadly in Morocco.

ingredients.text: Granulated sugar, honey, or confectioners’ sugar, for serving

method: Mix flour, yeast, salt, sugar, and enough water to make a very sticky, elastic batter-like dough. Beat or slap-fold for 8-10 minutes.
Cover and rise until tripled and bubbly, 60-90 minutes.
Heat oil to 350°F/175°C. Wet hands, pinch off a portion, form a hole with thumbs, stretch into a ring, and lower carefully into oil.
Fry 2-3 minutes per side until deeply golden and light. Drain and serve warm with sugar or honey.
accuracyNote: Sfenj is traditionally dairy-free and only lightly sweetened, if at all, before frying; Hanukkah significance comes from cooking in oil.

name: Trout with Preserved Lemon
originStatus: Contemporary North African Jewish/Moroccan-style preparation using classic preserved-lemon, olive, herb, and fish seasonings; trout is not the most traditional coastal species.

ingredients.text: 4 whole cleaned trout, 10-12 oz/285-340 g each
1 preserved lemon, pulp removed and rind julienned
1/2 cup green olives, rinsed and halved
1 small fennel bulb or onion, thinly sliced

method: Heat oven to 400°F/200°C. Score trout lightly and season inside and out. Rub with chermoula and rest 15 minutes.
Spread fennel or onion in a baking dish, add water and oil, and set trout on top.
Scatter preserved lemon and olives around the fish. Cover loosely and bake 15 minutes; uncover and cook 5-10 minutes more, until flesh is opaque and reaches about 145°F/63°C.
Spoon pan juices over the fish and serve.
accuracyNote: Rinse preserved lemon and olives before deciding how much additional salt the fish needs.

name: Couscous with Osban
originStatus: Tunisia and Libya; couscous steamed over a spicy broth in which osban tripe sausages cook with chickpeas and vegetables.

ingredients.text: 1 full batch uncooked osban from Recipe 54
3 carrots, 2 turnips, 1/2 cabbage, 2 zucchini, and 1 lb/450 g pumpkin, cut large

method: Fry onion, tomato paste, harissa, tabil, and paprika in oil. Add water and chickpeas and bring to a low simmer.
Add tied osban and simmer gently 1 hour. Add carrots, turnips, and cabbage.
Steam couscous over the broth in two or three stages, moistening and separating grains between steamings. Add zucchini and pumpkin for the final 20 minutes.
Verify the osban filling reaches 165°F/74°C. Slice it and arrange with vegetables over couscous; serve broth alongside.
accuracyNote: The osban both cooks in and seasons the couscous broth. Handle the filled casings gently to prevent rupture.

name: Fijuelas Fried Ribbons
originStatus: Moroccan Jewish fried ribbon pastry, also spelled fijuelas, fazuelos, or fiyuelas, commonly served for Purim and other celebrations.
method: Whisk eggs, oil, orange blossom water, and salt. Knead in enough flour to make a firm, smooth pasta-like dough. Rest covered 30 minutes.
Roll very thin by machine or rolling pin and cut into 1-inch/2.5-cm ribbons about 12 inches/30 cm long.
Heat oil to 350°F/175°C. Anchor one ribbon end around a fork and rotate the fork while frying to form a loose rose or coil. Fry until pale gold and crisp.
Warm honey, water, and lemon. Dip pastries briefly, drain, and garnish with sesame.
accuracyNote: Keep the dough thin and the frying color light; dark ribbons taste bitter and lose their delicate blistering.

name: Adafina Chickpea Pot
originStatus: Sephardic Sabbath stew with Iberian roots; adafina is an ancestral term related to Moroccan dafina. This version centers chickpeas, beef, grain, potatoes, and eggs.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g beef chuck or brisket
1 cup/190 g barley or wheat berries

method: Arrange drained chickpeas, meat, bone, onion, potatoes, grain in a loose cloth parcel, and eggs in a heavy pot.
Add spices, salt, oil, and boiling water. Simmer 10 minutes.
Cover tightly and bake at 225°F/107°C for 12-15 hours, maintaining enough liquid and continuous safe heat.
Serve eggs peeled and the grain parcel opened alongside the meat and chickpeas.
accuracyNote: Historical and regional adafina formulas are highly variable. This is a practical Sephardic archetype, not a reconstruction of one medieval household recipe.

name: Huevos Haminados
originStatus: Sephardic slow-cooked eggs, traditionally browned in the pot with hamin/dafina or cooked separately with onion skins and flavorings.

ingredients.text: 8 large eggs, shells scrubbed and uncracked
Water to cover by 2 inches/5 cm

method: Line a saucepan or small slow cooker with onion skins. Add eggs, tea, optional coffee, oil, salt, peppercorns, and water.
Bring to a gentle simmer for 10 minutes. Cover and cook on the lowest heat, in a 225°F/107°C oven, or in a slow cooker on low for 8-12 hours.
Keep eggs submerged, adding boiling water as needed.
Cool in cold water and peel. Whites should be beige to brown and yolks creamy-firm.
accuracyNote: The eggs may instead cook directly in dafina, where meat juices and spices deepen their color. Discard any egg cracked before cooking begins.

name: Lubia Black-Eyed Peas
originStatus: North African and Sephardic; black-eyed peas are eaten in several communities, including as a Rosh Hashanah symbolic food. This is a tomato-cumin stew.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g dried black-eyed peas, soaked 4 hours if desired

method: Soften onion in oil. Add garlic, tomato paste, tomatoes, and spices and cook 5 minutes.
Add peas and water. Simmer until tender, 35-60 minutes depending on age and soaking.
Add salt once peas are partly tender; stir in cilantro for the final 10 minutes.
Finish with lemon. Serve warm or at room temperature.
accuracyNote: “Lubia/loubia” can mean different beans in different Arabic dialects; this title specifically calls for black-eyed peas.

name: Tbikha Vegetable Stew
originStatus: Tunisia; tbikha names a category of cooked or stewed vegetable dishes, often spring legumes and greens. This meatless version uses fava beans, peas, artichokes, and chard.

ingredients.text: 1 bunch Swiss chard, stems and leaves chopped separately
1/2 cup chopped dill, parsley, and cilantro

method: Cook onion in oil, then add garlic, paste, harissa, tabil, turmeric, and salt. Fry 2 minutes.
Add water, artichokes, fava beans, chard stems, and chickpeas. Simmer 20 minutes.
Add peas, chard leaves, and herbs and cook until all vegetables are tender and sauce is reduced, 10-15 minutes.
Adjust with lemon juice.
accuracyNote: Tbikha is not one universal ingredient list; spring versions vary according to available legumes and greens.

name: Sfiria Chicken Croquettes
originStatus: Algeria, including Algerian Jewish cooking. The supplied name is misleading: sfiria are usually bread-and-cheese croquettes served in a chicken-and-chickpea sauce, rather than croquettes made primarily from chicken.

ingredients.text: 8 oz/225 g stale bread, soaked and squeezed dry

method: Brown chicken lightly in oil. Add onion, cinnamon, pepper, turmeric, salt, and water. Cover and simmer 30 minutes; add chickpeas.
Mix squeezed bread, cheese, eggs, parsley, cinnamon, and pepper. Form small ovals.
Fry at 350°F/175°C until golden and set, 3-4 minutes; drain.
When chicken reaches 165°F/74°C, add croquettes to the sauce for only 5-8 minutes so they absorb flavor without collapsing.
accuracyNote: Recipes differ in cheese and bread proportions, but the distinction between the chicken sauce and bread-based sfiria is central.

name: Mouna Sweet Bread
originStatus: Oran, Algeria; citrus- and orange-blossom-scented enriched bread strongly associated with Algerian, Pied-Noir, and Algerian Jewish foodways, especially spring and Easter traditions.

ingredients.text: 3/4 cup/180 ml warm milk or water
1/2 cup/120 ml olive or neutral oil
1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for glaze
Pearl sugar or sesame, for topping

method: Mix flour, yeast, sugar, salt, anise, and citrus zest. Add eggs, milk, oil, and orange blossom water and knead to a smooth, tacky dough, 10-12 minutes.
Cover and rise until doubled, 1 1/2-2 hours. Divide into two taut rounds on lined trays.
Proof until puffy, 45-75 minutes. Heat oven to 350°F/175°C.
Brush with egg wash, snip a cross or score the tops, add pearl sugar or sesame, and bake 30-40 minutes to 190°F/88°C internally. Cool fully.
accuracyNote: Mouna’s cultural ownership is shared and historically layered; it should not be reduced to a generic brioche or assigned exclusively to one religious community.

name: Pastel de Carne
originStatus: Broad Sephardic name for a meat pie; recipes vary from Ottoman pastry pies to Passover matzo or potato constructions. This is a dairy-free oil-pastry version.

ingredients.text: 1/2 cup/120 ml olive or neutral oil
1 1/2 lb/680 g ground beef or lamb

method: Mix flour and salt. Add oil and enough warm water to form a smooth medium-soft dough. Rest 30 minutes.
Cook onion in oil. Brown meat, add garlic and spices, and cook until dry. Cool and fold in parsley and optional eggs.
Heat oven to 375°F/190°C. Roll two-thirds of dough and line an oiled pie dish. Add filling. Cover with remaining dough, seal, vent, and brush with egg.
Bake until deep gold, 40-50 minutes. Rest 15 minutes before slicing.
accuracyNote: Because “pastel de carne” is a generic Ladino/Spanish descriptor, this formula is explicitly a representative Sephardic pie rather than a unique canonical dish.

name: Ktzitzot Fish Cakes
originStatus: Ktzitzot is Hebrew for patties; spiced fish cakes are common across Moroccan, Tunisian, and Libyan Jewish kitchens. This version is Moroccan-leaning.

ingredients.text: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed dry
1/2 cup/55 g fine breadcrumbs or matzo meal

method: Chop fish by hand or pulse briefly until coarse, not pasty. Mix with onion, garlic, herbs, spices, egg, and enough crumbs to hold together.
Chill 20 minutes, then form 16 patties.
Shallow-fry at 350°F/175°C for 2-3 minutes per side until golden and 145°F/63°C in the center.
Drain and serve with lemon, chraime sauce, or matbucha.
accuracyNote: Fish species and spice mixtures vary by diaspora community; coarse chopping keeps the cakes moist.

name: Marqa Batata Sweet-Sour
originStatus: The supplied title is not a single well-standardized dish name. This is a clearly labeled Tunisian-Jewish-style potato marqa balancing tomato, lemon, a little sugar, and warm spice.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g waxy potatoes, in large chunks

method: Soften onion in oil. Add garlic, paste, paprika, turmeric, caraway, cinnamon, and salt; fry 2 minutes.
Add water, potatoes, and chickpeas. Cover and simmer until potatoes are tender, 25-35 minutes.
Add 1 tbsp sugar and 2 tbsp lemon. Simmer uncovered until sauce clings to potatoes.
Adjust carefully with remaining sugar or lemon and add cilantro.
accuracyNote: “Sweet-sour” should remain restrained; this is an editorial reconstruction around documented marqa techniques, not claimed as a universally recognized formula.

name: Dafina with Kouclas
originStatus: Moroccan Jewish Sabbath stew with kouclas—seasoned grain, rice, meat, or bread dumplings cooked inside the pot.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g beef brisket or chuck
2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp cumin, 1/2 tsp cinnamon, 2 tsp salt
8 oz/225 g stale bread, soaked and squeezed dry

method: Mix kouclas ingredients. Form one large compact roll, wrap loosely in cheesecloth, and tie; or make two smaller dumplings.
Arrange dafina ingredients in a heavy pot and nestle in the wrapped kouclas. Add spices, oil, and boiling water.
Bring to a simmer 10 minutes, cover tightly, and bake at 225°F/107°C for 12-16 hours.
Unwrap and slice kouclas. Verify any meat in the dumpling reached at least 160°F/71°C.
accuracyNote: Kouclas vary greatly: bread, rice, wheat, and meat versions all exist. Wrapping protects a soft dumpling during overnight cooking.

name: Fritada de Espinaca
originStatus: Ottoman-Sephardic spinach-and-egg bake, related to quajado; not specifically Moroccan.

ingredients.text: 1 cup/100 g grated Parmesan, feta, or a mixture

method: Wilt spinach, cool, squeeze very dry, and chop. Heat oven to 350°F/175°C and oil a 9-inch baking dish.
Soften onion and scallions in oil. Combine with spinach, eggs, cheese, crumbs, salt, pepper, nutmeg, and lemon.
Spread evenly in the dish and bake until set and browned at the edges, 35-45 minutes.
Cool 15 minutes before cutting into squares.
accuracyNote: Removing spinach water is essential; a wet mixture will not set cleanly.

name: Debla Fried Roses
originStatus: Tunisia and Algeria; thin fried pastry ribbons shaped into roses or coils and coated in honey syrup. Related to but distinct from Moroccan fijuelas.
method: Knead flour, eggs, butter, vinegar, orange blossom water, salt, and enough water into a firm smooth dough. Rest 30 minutes.
Roll paper-thin and cut into long 1-inch/2.5-cm strips.
Fry at 350°F/175°C, winding each strip around a fork as it bubbles to form a flower, until pale gold.
Warm honey with lemon. Dip each debla, drain, and garnish.
accuracyNote: Vinegar helps limit oil absorption and encourages crispness; the pastry should remain delicate and light-colored.

name: Salona Sweet Fish
originStatus: Iraqi Jewish, not North African; fish in a tangy-sweet tomato, tamarind, and onion sauce traditionally associated with Sabbath meals.

ingredients.text: 2 lb/900 g firm fish fillets or steaks
2 tbsp tamarind concentrate, diluted to taste
1-2 tbsp brown sugar or date syrup

method: Season fish. Cook onions in oil until soft and golden, 15 minutes; add garlic.
Add tomatoes, paste, tamarind, sugar, turmeric, pepper, and water. Simmer 15-20 minutes and balance sweet against sour.
Nestle fish in sauce, cover, and simmer gently until just cooked and about 145°F/63°C, 8-15 minutes.
Add cilantro and rest 10 minutes before serving.
accuracyNote: Salona belongs to Iraqi Jewish cuisine. Its defining balance comes from tamarind acidity and restrained sweetness, not North African preserved lemon.

name: Bomba Rice Timbale
originStatus: No well-established North African or Sephardic canonical dish was found under this exact title. This is an editorial Spanish-Mediterranean rice timbale using bomba rice and North African seasonings.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 cups/300 g bomba or other short-grain rice
1/2 lb/225 g ground lamb or beef

method: Cook rice in stock until just tender and liquid is absorbed; cool slightly.
Cook onion and pepper in oil. Add meat and brown to 160°F/71°C. Add garlic, spices, salt, peas, and parsley; cool.
Heat oven to 375°F/190°C. Mix rice with beaten eggs. Oil and crumb six ramekins.
Line each with rice, add meat filling, and cap with rice. Bake 25 minutes, rest 10 minutes, and invert.
accuracyNote: This is intentionally labeled as a modern construction. It should not be presented as an inherited North African Jewish recipe without a family or documentary source.

name: Ojja with Merguez
originStatus: Tunisia; spicy tomato-pepper stew with eggs, here enriched with merguez sausage.
method: Brown merguez in a skillet until nearly cooked; remove and slice. Confirm sausage ultimately reaches 160°F/71°C.
Cook onion and pepper in the rendered fat and oil until soft. Add garlic, paste, harissa, tabil, and caraway.
Add tomatoes and water and simmer until thick, 15 minutes. Return sausage.
Crack eggs into the sauce and stir them lightly for a rustic ojja texture, or leave whole. Cover until set. Garnish with parsley.
accuracyNote: Ojja is often more vigorously spiced and less chunky than shakshuka; eggs may be stirred directly into the sauce.

name: Kaak Anise Rings
originStatus: Tunisia and North African Jewish baking; crisp or tender ring biscuits scented with anise, sesame, citrus, or orange blossom water.

ingredients.text: 1/2 cup/120 ml olive or neutral oil

method: Heat oven to 350°F/175°C. Mix dry ingredients, anise, sesame, and zest.
Whisk eggs, oil, and orange blossom water. Mix into dry ingredients, adding only enough water for a firm, smooth dough.
Roll walnut-size pieces into ropes and join ends into rings. Arrange on lined trays and brush with egg wash if desired.
Bake until golden and dry, 20-25 minutes. Cool completely.
accuracyNote: “Kaak” is a broad Arabic word for ring breads and biscuits; texture and seasoning differ across communities.

name: Loubia b’Dersa
originStatus: Algeria; white beans cooked in a red garlic-chile dersa sauce.

ingredients.text: 1 lb/450 g dried white beans, soaked overnight

method: Pound garlic with paprika, cayenne, cumin, and 1/2 tsp salt to make dersa.
Fry dersa gently in oil 30 seconds. Add tomato paste and grated tomato and cook 3 minutes.
Add drained beans and water. Simmer partially covered until beans are creamy-tender, 60-90 minutes. Add remaining salt once partly tender.
Reduce to a thick stew and finish with vinegar or lemon and parsley.
accuracyNote: This Algerian version foregrounds dersa and may contain little or no onion.

name: Terfess Desert Truffle Stew
originStatus: Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Saharan regions; terfess or desert truffles are seasonal fungi cooked with meat or in light aromatic sauces.

ingredients.text: 1 1/2 lb/680 g culinary desert truffles, thoroughly cleaned and peeled if needed
